claims.text: A combined atomistic-simulation and in situ calorimetry protocol can rapidly and accurately determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, melting volume change, and selected liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across single-phase HEAs.
Hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations can be calibrated using local-distortion and chemical-short-range-order measurements.
Careful compositional control can minimize secondary phases and produce well-defined single-phase HEAs.
Calibrated atomistic simulations can compute fusion thermodynamic properties.
High-temperature differential scanning calorimetry and dilatometry can validate or adjust simulated fusion-property predictions.

Prior work has combined experiments and first-principles hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics to determine chemical short-range order, bond lengths, and local atomic distortions in a single-phase HEA family.
Controlled experimental atmospheres prevent oxidation during high-temperature measurements.
Appropriate heating rates allow the tested HEAs to approach equilibrium.
Local atomic distortions and chemical short-range order influence fusion thermodynamics.
Local atomic distortions and chemical short-range order influence the effective configurational entropy of an HEA.
Local bonding variations correlate with macroscopic melting and liquid-state properties.
Adjusting simulation parameters with in situ measurements minimizes errors caused by intrinsic configurational entropy.
The method will predict fusion properties within approximately 5–10% of direct experimental measurements.
The method will efficiently map melting temperatures and related thermodynamic quantities across the HEA family.
The predicted fusion properties will be sensitive to compositional adjustments.
Conventional high-temperature measurements without simulation guidance often lack efficiency or fail to capture full configurational complexity.
The approach may not be effective for multiphase HEAs or alloys with extreme chemical segregation.
The quantitative accuracy depends on simulation-potential quality and experimental calibration accuracy.
